what_its_for: Dacomitinib is a cancer medicine used to treat a type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It is used when the cancer has spread to other parts of the body (metastatic) and has a certain gene change (mutation) called EGFR exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R substitution. Your doctor will do a test to make sure this medicine is right for your type of cancer.
how_to_take: Take dacomitinib by mouth (swallow the tablet whole) with or without food. Take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do not crush, chew, or split the tablet. If you vomit after taking a dose, do NOT take another dose — just take your next scheduled dose at the regular time.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 45 mg once daily. Your doctor may lower your dose to 30 mg or 15 mg once daily if you have side effects. Always follow the exact dose your doctor prescribes. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and there are MORE than 12 hours until your next scheduled dose, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If there are 12 hours or LESS until your next dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store dacomitinib tablets at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Protect from moisture and heat. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking antacids (like Tums or Maalox) within 3 hours before or 3 hours after taking dacomitinib, as they can make the medicine less effective. Avoid proton pump inhibitors (medicines like omeprazole or pantoprazole) unless your doctor says it is okay — these can reduce how well the medicine works. Avoid prolonged sun exposure and use sunscreen, as your skin may become more sensitive to sunlight. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, including herbal products, because some medicines can interact with dacomitinib.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe or worsening shortness of breath, new or worsening cough, or fever (these could be signs of a serious lung problem called interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis); severe skin rash, blistering, or peeling; signs of eye problems such as eye pain, redness, vision changes, or increased sensitivity to light; severe diarrhea that does not improve with over-the-counter medicines; mouth sores that are very painful or make it hard to eat or drink; any signs of infection (fever, chills, unusual tiredness). Also let your doctor know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
when_it_works: Dacomitinib does not cure cancer, but it works to slow down or stop cancer growth. Some people notice improvements within the first few weeks, but it may take several months to see the full benefit. Your doctor will schedule regular check-ups and scans to see how well the medicine is working for you. Keep taking your medicine every day, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Dacomitinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 17 days after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 31 days after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for at least 17 days after the last dose. Liver or Kidney Problems: Tell your doctor if you have liver or kidney disease, as your dose may need to be adjusted. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children. Older Adults: Older adults (65 and older) can take this medicine, but they may be more sensitive to side effects — talk to your doctor about any concerns.
